name: David Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. This conversation is confidential. What is your workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m David Ibrahim, 58, and I operate a rock breaker at a large mine. I inspect the hydraulic lines before the shift, then break oversize rocks so the haul trucks can clear the bay. I like a job where a good operator can keep the whole line moving, though the noise is hard on the ears.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares your life away from the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Samira works part time at a bakery, and our two sons are grown and out on their own. I have a vocational certificate and enough saved for about five months of our expenses. We help with meals at our community hall, but my mine wage pays most of our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a computer saving the stores clerk ten minutes is no threat to the breaker. I sometimes use an AI tool to find a manual page, after the younger operators show me how. I still want the fitter to sign off a hydraulic repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d welcome another stretch of regular shifts so Samira and I can improve our savings. Her bakery hours change around holidays, and five months of bills is useful but short of retirement money. I would keep working until the figures say we can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d continue checking the hydraulic lines before each shift and breaking the rocks assigned to me. This winter I’d put part of any overtime pay into our savings account. In the first year after the minor software changes, I’d try the new stores lookup after another operator shows it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my job and curious about a quicker way to find a part number. I would not hurry to buy a new device for it. Samira’s variable hours are a more immediate concern than the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the stores lookup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check the part number against the paper manual and ask the fitter if it matches our machine. If it gets two common seals right, I might use it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much overtime money would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of whatever overtime I actually get would go into our savings account. I cannot budget overtime before the mine offers it, so I keep our ordinary bills on base pay.

say: I’d say a quicker **stores lookup** could help without replacing the breaker operator.
I’d still require a **fitter** to approve hydraulic repairs.
think: I want continued **mine shifts** to build savings before retirement.
Samira’s **bakery hours** vary, and five months of bills is limited.
do: Check **hydraulic lines** and run the breaker as assigned.
Save half of any **overtime pay** actually received.
Try the **stores lookup** after checking part numbers with the fitter.
feel: **Calm** about the job and curious about a proven lookup tool.
S0.quote: I cannot budget overtime before the mine offers it, so I keep our ordinary bills on base pay.
fieldNote: David accepts **proven digital tools** gradually and keeps hydraulic repairs under a fitter’s direct approval.
His savings plan uses only **actual overtime** because bakery hours vary and regular mine pay covers household bills.

steps.text: Keep inspecting hydraulic lines and operating the rock breaker
Save half of any overtime pay actually received
Try the AI stores lookup after checking part numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the ordering and scheduling staff will feel this first, before robots can break rock for us. I would ask the mine to show the crew its new parts system before turning off the old one. An apprenticeship should still teach a person how to spot a leaking line, not just press approve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might gain time if parts come faster, but I worry that a smaller stores team means nobody checks the order twice. I expect my breaker shifts to continue for now. If Samira’s bakery uses automated ordering, I do not know whether her part-time hours change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the stores lead next week to show me how the AI order suggestions are checked. I’d use the system beside the parts book for a month and report wrong seal numbers. In the first year I’d keep my breaker shifts and help our apprentice learn the physical line checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy because other people’s work is moving quickly. I can learn a tool once somebody proves it, but I do not want the shop or the mine to build a schedule around wrong numbers. Samira and I would watch her hours closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a wrong seal number cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The breaker could sit idle until another delivery arrives, and a fitter might be sent out twice. I’d show the stores lead the manual page and the old seal before placing a new order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Samira to leave the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she likes her shifts and they bring in money. We would first see what her manager actually changes rather than treat a news story as a dismissal letter.

say: I’d say **stores and scheduling** change before hands-on rock breaking.
I’d keep **physical line checks** in an apprentice’s training.
think: My **breaker shifts** likely continue, though fewer stores checks could delay repairs.
Samira’s **bakery hours** might change if ordering becomes automated.
do: Ask the stores lead how **AI orders** are checked.
Compare suggested **seal numbers** with the parts book for a month.
Keep breaker shifts and show the apprentice **line checks**.
feel: **Uneasy** about shifting office work and uncertain household hours.
S1.quote: An apprenticeship should still teach a person how to spot a leaking line, not just press approve.
fieldNote: David’s interest in **ordering software** comes from delays caused by wrong parts, a concrete problem for the breaker.
His own shifts appear stable, but **Samira’s hours** could shrink if bakery ordering work changes.

steps.text: Compare AI seal suggestions with the parts book for a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 may take the ordering desk, but rock-breaking robots reach our machines around 2031. Three years of wages matter, and the mine should put real dates on paper. If the equipment can work as well as a person, management may stop paying operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when full AI reaches the office and 63 when robots can do my hands-on work. I expected several more years of wages to put aside; five months of expenses will not replace them. Samira’s part-time bakery pay would cover only a portion of our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask payroll for my retirement statement and the mine for its planned machine purchase dates. I’d apply for an advertised heavy-equipment service role if its training is paid, since I know the breaker but cannot afford unpaid months. In 2029 I’d keep taking breaker shifts, and I’d cancel the planned room renovation to leave cash in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the gap between the mine’s timetable and my own. I have some savings and could ask about other jobs, but a service role might also be changed by robots. I would not tell our sons we are ruined before I know the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on paid training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course itself might help, but Samira’s bakery wage cannot carry the rent and food while I train for free. I’d take a paid opening with a stated contract and ask what work it leads to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does canceling the room mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We planned to replace the worn floor in the back room. We can live with that floor longer, and I would explain the delay to Samira before calling the contractor.

say: I’d ask the mine for written **robot purchase dates**.
I’d tell coworkers that **2031 robots** could end operator wages.
think: At **63**, I could lose years of wages I meant to save.
Five months of savings and Samira’s **part-time pay** would not cover a long gap.
do: Request my **retirement statement** and machine dates.
Apply for a paid **service role** if advertised.
Keep breaker shifts in **2029** and cancel the room renovation.
feel: **Anxious** about a shortened earning period, while still able to ask about work.
S2.quote: Three years of wages matter, and the mine should put real dates on paper.
fieldNote: David counts the **three-year gap** before robots as real earnings but cannot rely on it for a full retirement cushion.
He will seek **paid training** through an actual service vacancy because unpaid months would strain the household.

steps.text: Keep operating the rock breaker in 2029 if shifts remain
Apply for an advertised heavy-equipment service role with paid training
Cancel the planned back-room floor renovation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives a working family time to count its money, if the mine shares its machine orders. Full thinking AI in 2031 would change the desks first; breaker robots around 2034 could end my shift at 66. I would want operators who trained apprentices to be treated fairly if that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be ready to retire at 66, but I have not seen a firm figure for what we would receive. Samira might choose fewer bakery hours by then, and I cannot count on our grown sons paying our bills. I would rather work a little longer than take an exit payment I do not understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a retirement adviser to put our savings, bills and any pension entitlement on one page this year. I’d continue the breaker job while I can and apply for a paid apprentice trainer opening if the mine advertises one. In 2032 I’d check any exit offer against that page before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, though the warning makes it manageable. A real adviser’s figures would settle more than a speech about the future. I would still want to finish work with some choice of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train apprentices if robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the mine hires them and pays me for that work. People still need safe hands during the changeover, but I would ask how long the trainer post lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the adviser says retirement is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira and I would keep our regular spending tight and I would hold onto paid breaker shifts if offered. We would tell the sons the truth, but I would not make them the plan.

say: I’d say **five years** allows a proper household calculation.
I’d want fair terms for operators who taught **apprentices**.
think: At **66**, I might retire if our actual income covers bills.
Samira’s future **bakery hours** and any pension amount remain uncertain.
do: Ask a **retirement adviser** to list income and bills together.
Keep paid breaker shifts and apply for an advertised **trainer opening**.
Compare any **2032 exit offer** with the household figures.
feel: **Uneasy** about the final working date but able to plan with figures.
S3.quote: I would rather work a little longer than take an exit payment I do not understand.
fieldNote: David does not treat age **66** as an automatic retirement date and wants a documented household calculation.
He would consider **paid apprentice training** if the mine opens a real post with a known term.

steps.text: Keep operating the breaker while paid shifts are offered
Apply for a paid apprentice trainer opening if the mine advertises one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that ten years is long enough to pass down sound equipment habits. Full thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I’d be 68; rock-breaking robots follow around 2039, when I’d be 71. I hope to be out of the breaker seat by then, with younger operators properly trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not plan to work to 71, but I cannot yet promise we can afford to stop at 68. A decade gives Samira and me time to save and decide whether her bakery shifts are for income or enjoyment. I would rather hand over a healthy machine than leave a worn line for a robot or a new operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d set an annual date with Samira to review savings and retirement income, and I’d keep paid shifts while my health allows. I’d put any overtime pay we do not need for bills into savings. In 2037 I’d decide whether to retire from the breaker after comparing our monthly income with housing, food and medicine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about the robot date and more focused on my health. Ten years is enough time to prepare if we actually use the calendar. I would still be sad to see nobody at the controls one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want a younger operator to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hose can look sound until you wipe it and see the wet line under the fitting. I’d show a new operator that check in person if the foreman gives us the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you afford retirement at 68 if the bakery stays part time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know until we see the statement and savings trend. If the figures are short in 2037, I would ask for the paid work still available instead of announcing retirement.

say: I’d say a **decade** is enough to pass on safe equipment habits.
I hope to leave the **breaker seat** before robots reach it around 2039.
think: At **68** in 2036, retirement still depends on our actual income.
Samira’s bakery shifts may remain **necessary income**.
do: Review **retirement income** with Samira each year.
Keep paid shifts and save unused **overtime pay**.
Compare **2037 bills** with income before choosing a retirement date.
feel: **Calm** about the late robot date, with health and finances still important.
S4.quote: I would rather hand over a healthy machine than leave a worn line for a robot or a new operator.
fieldNote: David expects to leave the **breaker seat** before robots reach it, but refuses to claim retirement is affordable yet.
His **yearly review** ties savings and bakery income to ordinary bills rather than a fixed age alone.

steps.text: Keep paid breaker shifts while health and mine work permit
Save overtime pay not needed for household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most; robots could end my breaker work at 63 while I still need the wage. I’d want written purchase dates, a real paid training vacancy and clear retirement figures. Samira and I can make a careful decision when we know what is actually offered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether anyone gets paid time to teach the next operator. I can show a young worker where a hydraulic leak hides, but not if every shift is timed down to the minute. An apprenticeship needs hours beside the machine.

headlineQuote: An apprenticeship needs hours beside the machine.
portrait: David, **58**, operates a rock breaker and checks hydraulic lines before each shift.
His mine wage supports Samira’s variable **bakery pay** and a five-month savings cushion.
He tests **AI tools** after checking results with a fitter or manual.
He would seek a real **paid service post** if fast robots threaten his remaining earning years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries David most because breaker robots around 2031 could end his wages at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Written **purchase dates**, a paid training vacancy and clear retirement figures would help him decide.
